entries.subject: An isolated working timber mitre lock gate mechanism with visible controlled water.
entries.brief: ONE PAIR OF HISTORICAL WOODEN MITRE LOCK GATES as a compact isolated FUNCTIONAL APPARATUS, shown in three-quarter view. The two broad timber gate leaves meet to form a shallow V pointing upstream; their edges connect properly, dark iron straps and hinges reinforce warm brown oak planks. Two balance beams extend from the gate tops toward their respective outer hinge posts, visibly attached. A SMALL bounded wedge of dull green-grey WATER sits just upstream behind the gates, with a lower visible water patch immediately downstream. ONE inset sluice paddle near the bottom is slightly raised and a small clear stream of water flows through its actual rectangular opening into the downstream water. The water belongs to the mechanism, not a scenic canal. Only minimal attached side hinge posts, no long masonry lock chamber, landscape, vegetation, sky, buildings, towpath, boat, human, scenic baseplate, frame or floor. This is a TECHNOLOGY object icon, never a building vignette. No detached beams, waterfall through solid timber, modern railings or neon blue water.

refs.title: How canal locks work — Canal & River Trust
refs.note: Gate and water-control principles; isolated apparatus is a simplified visual adaptation.

refs.title: Salterhebble Top Lock — Historic England
refs.note: Circa 1779 timber gates and balance beams; image search used as construction reference.

entries.subject: Five newspaper copies in a fan with authentic French, American and Qing Chinese publication names.
entries.brief: Real, readable publication mastheads replace abstract top bands. The paper fan and almost-white materials are preserved.

refs.title: Le Figaro (Paris, 1826) — BnF
refs.note: Primary catalogue: publication 1826–1834. Title only, not a copy of a modern logo or issue. Some publications had formats different from the stylized folded broadsheet.

refs.title: Le Constitutionnel (1815) — BnF
refs.note: Primary catalogue search result verifies 1815–1817 title. Direct open failed; no exact scan was copied.

refs.title: National Intelligencer — Library of Congress
refs.note: Catalogue gives foundation in 1800 and title change in 1810 to National Intelligencer. Use publication name, not reproduced articles.

refs.title: 京報 — Taiwan Ministry of Education dictionary
refs.note: Official dictionary identifies Qing-era Beijing print publication carrying court news, not a modern independent mass-market daily. Traditional spelling 京報.

refs.title: 京報 rare-book catalogue — National Central Library
refs.note: Catalogue search result describes 1904–1905 copies; evidence of name and print practice, NOT an early-19th-century dated physical specimen.

entries.prompt:
Use case: text-localization.
Asset type: one transparent painted TECHNOLOGY icon for Victoria 3 / 1776 Age of Revolutions.
Input image 1: EDIT TARGET, the existing five folded newspapers in a fan.
Primary request: replace the abstract grey masthead bands with REAL, CORRECTLY SPELLED newspaper names. This is now a multilingual fan of different publications, not five copies of one edition.
Mastheads, exact allowed text:
- Front/right foremost newspaper: "LE FIGARO", large dark nineteenth-century serif type.
- Newspaper immediately behind it on the left: "NATIONAL INTELLIGENCER", on two centered lines if necessary, both complete.
- Tall central/rear newspaper whose upper edge is clearly visible: "京報", exactly these TWO Traditional Chinese characters, 京 then 報, in bold period woodblock-style Chinese lettering.
- Leftmost visible newspaper: "LE CONSTITUTIONNEL", complete period serif text; two lines if needed.
- Fifth remaining newspaper: another copy titled "LE FIGARO"; partial obscuration of this repeated title is acceptable.
These are the only readable words or characters. Spell all four distinct mastheads correctly and make each distinct name clearly visible at large size. Use only the authentic publication names as text, NOT copied logos or a facsimile of a specific historical issue. No invented article headlines, dates, prices, modern slogans, tiny random words or watermark.
Body printing: retain the narrow neutral charcoal ink-column pattern; for the Chinese newspaper use vertically arranged abstract small ink marks to suggest Chinese columns. Body copy is an abstract printing texture, not legible fictional news text.
Preserve: the compact open FAN arrangement of exactly five thin folded period newspapers, paper edges, curls, folds, nearly white ivory color, matte fine paper grain, restrained painted volume, upper-left light and natural shading. No new machine, gear, accessories, background, people, floor, cast shadow, frame or medallion. If essential, slightly uncover the upper portion of a newspaper to show its complete masthead, while keeping the same five-paper fan silhouette and coherent paper overlaps.
Output: genuinely transparent alpha around the whole object and through all gaps; full silhouette inside generous margins on a square high-resolution canvas, no edge cropping. No blue cast, sepia filter, photocopy scan background or modern magazine photographs. This is a conceptual period publication icon, not a claim that all editions shared this physical size.

entries.subject: Two clasped hands as a compact painted symbol of mutual aid.
entries.brief: ONE compact, plainly understandable HANDSHAKE: TWO human hands clasped firmly in mutual aid, shown as a coherent pair of hands and short wrists with simple nineteenth-century cloth cuffs. Anatomically correct grip, thumbs properly opposed over the grasp, five fingers per hand, no extra fingers, no fused or severed anatomy. One off-white linen cuff and one subdued brown woven cuff, both attached naturally to their wrists. Modest natural skin tones and restrained painted highlights, not gold embossed metal. Strong broad joined-hands silhouette; entire cuffs included and softly finished within the object silhouette, no edge cropping. This is a CONCEPTUAL TECHNOLOGY ICON, not a poster, seal or bronze badge. No coin, circular emblem, laurel wreath, stars, flags, hammer/sickle, slogan, modern suit sleeve, gold halo, blood, building, people or background. The handshake communicates cooperation and solidarity, not a precise portrait or exact national emblem. Human hands are the deliberate primary subject here, overriding the generic no-people/no-hands rule used for machines.

refs.title: Mutual aid banner, 1890–1899 — Italian Ministry of Culture
refs.note: Later nineteenth-century clasped-hands emblem as solidarity motif, not copied banner or proof of a unique early socialist insignia.

refs.title: Workers' symbolism — Museum Wales
refs.note: Clasped hands are among working-class symbols; conceptual adaptation rather than exact era-specific badge.
